newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE--Brazil traders wary of further export cuts.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Brazil traders wary of further export cuts.

text.p: A statement by Colombian and African coffee officials that exports by a group of producers needed to be cut by around 2.5 million bags in first half of 1997 was given a cool reception by Brazilian traders.
"I don't think that people will see as a reason to do this," one trader at a major exporter said.

An African delegation which met Wednesday with Colombian coffee officials in Bogota is to hold talks with Brazilian government representatives on December 13 and are expected to ask for Brazil's support in limiting exports further.
Under a plan agreed by members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in May, member shipments in the first six months of 1997 should not exceed 26.28 million 60-kg bags.

Many traders interpreted the announcement as a sign that Colombia would at any rate find it difficult to fulfill its quota for the coming six months and so is hoping prices will rise higher by announcing a reduction.
"It is very easy for Colombia to say there should be a reduction. It appears to be showing signs it does not have the coffee it says it has," one trader said.

There has already been talk that Brazil will be hard pushed to make its quota of six million bags in the first half of next year given strong internal demand. But its limit can be met if the government auctions sufficient stocks.
Given a forecast trade deficit of up to $5 billion this year and a government drive to boost exports, traders see it unlikely officials would agree to place a further cap on sales.
"Exports are very important currently for the whole country," said Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Association.
For one key exporter, any cut would only really be appropriate for robusta coffee exports.
"This has absolutely nothing to do with arabica exports...In arabica coffee we are already beginning to see a shortage," said Jair Coser, president of leading coffee exporter Unicafe.
Traders do not expect any commitment from Brazil at tomorrow's meeting but are watching to see if the push from Africa and Colombia will lead to an emergency ACPC meeting.

"The conclusion of the (last) ACPC meeting in Costa Rica was that if we saw the need to take further action, then the president has the right to call an emergency meeting as soon as possible," said Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation.

There had been some talk at a recent industry gathering in Brazil attended by ACPC president Rubens Barbosa that the ACPC could hold a meeting just ahead of an international coffee seminar in Rio de Janeiro at the end of January, Coser said.
"But now it looks as if that would be too late and that the push will be for a meeting in December," he added.
